source_title: Growth momentum holds despite shocks: RBI Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta - Business Standard
source_excerpt: India’s economic growth momentum has remained strong despite a series of shocks, including high US tariffs, surging oil prices, deficient monsoon rainfall and capital outflows, said Poonam Gupta, Deputy Governor at the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), citing the economy’s diversified growth base and improved policy response. The economy grew 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of the current financial year, with momentum continuing into the second quarter, raising expectations of upgrades to growth forecasts, she said at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit on Tuesday. “Such was the momentum seen in the economy, but interestingly, that momentum is continuing up to the second quarter,” Gupta said, pointing to indicators including tax collections, bank credit growth, exports, Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) readings and industrial and infrastructure activity. She said India had faced a wide range of shocks, and also witnessed high capital outflows as global investors shifted towards artificial intelligence-related activities. “…I would like to believe that India has been subjected to more shocks than perhaps any other economy in the world. You name the shock and India was potentially impacted,” she said. India would need to improve its competitiveness in new sectors, keep pace with technological changes and invest in human capital to sustain growth of 7 per cent and move towards 8 per cent or higher, said Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta, at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit, on Tuesday. She compared the shift to moving from an A grade to an A-plus, saying it would require a disproportionate amount of effort. “If this global environment becomes better, if not right away in the next one year, another 50 basis points to 1 percentage point growth will come just from there,” she said. Gupta said India’s growth story was supported by several drivers rather than depending on one or two sources of growth. Economies that rely heavily on natural resources, a particular export market, remittances or favourable demographics can be more vulnerable when those sources come under pressure, she said. “India has all of the above, plus much more,” Gupta said, referring to the range of factors supporting the economy. She added that India’s growth was broad-based across regions and sectors and supported by rising productivity. The resilience also reflected improvements in policy frameworks, with a firm focus on macroeconomic and financial stability. The RBI Deputy Governor said the response to shocks needed to be assessed not only in terms of their immediate impact on growth but also in terms of how policy decisions helped the economy adjust over time. Gupta said India had become less vulnerable to some economic shocks as a result of deliberate policy action and adaptation. She cited oil price shocks and deficient rainfall as examples of disruptions to which the economy had been more sensitive in the past. “And just as the rest of the world, over time, due to conscious policy actions and adaptation, the economy has become less sensitive to some of the shocks,” she said. Gupta cautioned against the temptation to respond to economic shocks with short-term measures, saying policymakers needed to maintain a longer-term perspective. “When confronting such shocks, there is a temptation. Everybody has a temptation to break short-term retreats, and one has to restrain oneself. The focus has to be on the medium and long term,” she said. Gupta said the way shocks were managed also mattered, pointing to policy certainty, greater engagement with stakeholders, better communication and timely action as factors that had helped India navigate recent challenges. She stressed that the outcomes could not be attributed to the central bank or a single government department, but reflected coordination across different parts of the economy and government. “And more is the way the shocks have been managed, certainly this time around, with policy certainty, more engagement with stakeholders, better communication and timely action, and what I call all of the system approach,” she said. “If you think it’s only the central bank or the ministry of food which have made these outcomes possible… It has been the effort of many, many stakeholders. Effort of the private sector, households, state governments, minister of external affairs, minister of agriculture, (and) department of consumer affairs.” She said the collective response across institutions and stakeholders had helped make the outcomes possible, emphasising that resilience depended on more than the actions of any one institution. Gupta’s remarks placed India’s growth performance in the context of both its economic structure and its policy response. A diversified domestic economy provides multiple sources of growth, while policy certainty and coordination can help reduce the impact of shocks. She said the challenge for policymakers was to preserve this resilience by maintaining macroeconomic and financial stability and keeping the focus on the medium and long term. On public finances, Gupta said India was better placed than many economies, where debt ratios had risen since the Covid-19 pandemic. Global public debt stood at about 94 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025 and is projected to reach 100 per cent by 2029, according to the IMF’s April 2026 Fiscal Monitor. She said India’s general government debt-to-GDP ratio was projected to decline from around 84 per cent in 2025 to 75 per cent by 2041-42. Improving the quality of fiscal expenditure, greater transparency and a debt composition that keeps borrowing costs contained would support the country’s fiscal position.About inflation, she said global price pressures remained exposed to oil prices, weather-related disruptions and higher shipping, logistics and insurance costs. The International Monetary Fund’s (IMF’s) inflation projections cited by Gupta put global headline inflation at 4.7 per cent in 2026, up from 4.1 per cent in 2025, before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027. For India, inflation was projected to rise from 2 per cent in 2025 to 5 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.4 per cent in 2027, she said. Central banks need to distinguish temporary supply shocks from more persistent price pressures while remaining alert to second-round effects through wages and inflation expectations. The RBI Deputy Governor said monetary policy should remain focused on price stability, with central banks taking timely action to bring inflation back to target and prevent temporary shocks from becoming persistent. The flexibility built into inflation-targeting frameworks, including tolerance bands, had helped central banks tailor their responses to specific challenges, she said. On the global front, Gupta said the financial sector faced three emerging risks: A potential fall in artificial intelligence (AI)-related asset prices if investments and profits disappointed; a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields amid renewed inflation; and cyber threats that could pose systemic risks to increasingly digital and interconnected financial services. Gupta said the financial sector had held up well globally so far, but risks highlighted in the IMF’s Global Financial Stability Report warranted attention. “A fall in the prices of AI-related assets, if investments and profits in AI prove weaker or less profitable than expected,” was one of the risks, Gupta added, and also flagged the possibility of “a sharp increase in sovereign bond yields from renewed inflation” and warned that cyber threats were becoming a systemic risk as financial services grew more digital and interconnected.
hi_body:
भारतीय रिजर्व बैंक (RBI) की डिप्टी गवर्नर पूनम गुप्ता ने कहा है कि उच्च अमेरिकी टैरिफ, बढ़ते तेल की कीमतें, कम मानसून वर्षा और पूंजी बहिर्वाह जैसे कई वैश्विक और घरेलू झटकों के बावजूद भारत की आर्थिक वृद्धि की गति मजबूत बनी हुई है।

बिजनेस स्टैंडर्ड बीएफएसआई इनसाइट समिट में बोलते हुए, गुप्ता ने बताया कि चालू वित्त वर्ष की पहली तिमाही में अर्थव्यवस्था 7.8 प्रतिशत की दर से बढ़ी, और यह गति दूसरी तिमाही में भी जारी रही। उन्होंने कर संग्रह, बैंक ऋण वृद्धि, निर्यात, क्रय प्रबंधक सूचकांक (PMI) और औद्योगिक गतिविधियों जैसे संकेतकों का हवाला दिया।

## आर्थिक लचीलेपन के मुख्य कारक

* **विविध विकास आधार:** भारत एकल क्षेत्र के बजाय कई आर्थिक चालकों पर निर्भर करता है, जिससे संवेदनशीलता कम होती है।
* **बेहतर नीतिगत ढांचा:** बेहतर नीतिगत निश्चितता, समय पर कार्रवाई और हितधारकों की सहभागिता ने झटकों को कम करने में मदद की है।
* **कम संवेदनशीलता:** समय के साथ किए गए नीतिगत समायोजन से अर्थव्यवस्था तेल की कीमतों और कम बारिश जैसे व्यवधानों के प्रति कम संवेदनशील हुई है।

## भविष्य की वृद्धि और चुनौतियां

गुप्ता ने इस बात पर जोर दिया कि 7 प्रतिशत की वृद्धि को बनाए रखने और 8 प्रतिशत या उससे अधिक की ओर बढ़ने के लिए नए क्षेत्रों में प्रतिस्पर्धा में सुधार, तकनीकी बदलावों और मानव पूंजी में निवेश की आवश्यकता है। उन्होंने यह भी उल्लेख किया कि भारत के सामान्य सरकारी ऋण-से-जीडीपी अनुपात में गिरावट का अनुमान है।

मुद्रास्फीति और वैश्विक जोखिमों के संबंध में, गुप्ता ने तेल की कीमतों, मौसम के व्यवधानों और शिपिंग लागतों से संभावित दबावों की ओर इशारा किया। उन्होंने अंतर्राष्ट्रीय मुद्रा कोष (IMF) की ग्लोबल फाइनेंशियल स्टेबिलिटी रिपोर्ट में उल्लिखित उभरते वैश्विक वित्तीय जोखिमों पर भी प्रकाश डाला।

## सत्यापन कैसे करें

इच्छुक पाठक भारतीय रिजर्व बैंक (RBI) द्वारा जारी आधिकारिक प्रकाशनों, मौद्रिक नीति रिपोर्टों और बयानों की समीक्षा कर सकते हैं या व्यापक आर्थिक संदर्भों के लिए अंतर्राष्ट्रीय मुद्रा कोष (IMF) की रिपोर्टों का संदर्भ ले सकते हैं।

en_body:
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta stated that India's economic growth momentum has remained strong despite facing numerous global and domestic shocks, including high US tariffs, surging oil prices, deficient monsoon rainfall, and capital outflows.

Speaking at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit, Gupta reported that the economy grew by 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of the current financial year, with positive momentum extending into the second quarter. She noted that indicators such as tax collections, bank credit growth, exports, Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) readings, and industrial and infrastructure activity support this ongoing trend.

## Key Factors Behind Economic Resilience

* **Diversified Growth Base:** India relies on multiple economic drivers rather than a single sector, reducing vulnerability.
* **Improved Policy Frameworks:** Enhanced policy certainty, timely actions, and stakeholder engagement have helped mitigate shocks.
* **Reduced Sensitivity:** Conscious policy adjustments over time have made the economy less sensitive to disruptions like oil price volatility and deficient rainfall.

## Future Growth and Challenges

Gupta emphasized that sustaining a growth rate of 7 per cent and aiming for 8 per cent or higher requires improving competitiveness in new sectors, adapting to technological changes, and investing in human capital. She also noted that India's general government debt-to-GDP ratio is projected to decline from around 84 per cent in 2025 to 75 per cent by 2041-42, placing the country in a relatively favorable fiscal position compared to global trends.

Regarding inflation and global risks, Gupta pointed to potential pressures from oil prices, weather disruptions, and shipping costs. She also highlighted emerging global financial risks outlined in the IMF's Global Financial Stability Report, including potential declines in AI-related asset prices, sharp rises in sovereign bond yields, and systemic cyber threats.

## How to Verify

Interested readers can review official publications, monetary policy reports, and statements released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) or consult the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) Fiscal Monitor and Global Financial Stability Report for broader economic contexts.
en_title: RBI Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta Highlights Economic Resilience Despite Multiple Shocks
